extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy and literature; writers interested in moral-political storytelling and education
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing moral and political allegories (city-building narratives, character thought-experiments) and for shaping stories used in education, especially for children and guardian-figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolate characters at moral extremes for clear judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the unjust man be entirely unjust, and the just man entirely just; nothing is to be taken away from either of them, and both are to be perfectly furnished for the work of their respective lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use thought-experiment technique: construct two characters pushed to their uttermost extremes (one perfectly just, the other perfectly unjust) so that their lives can be compared without confounding factors. Ensure each is internally consistent and fully equipped to pursue his nature (skills, resources, ability to recover from mistakes). This clarifies what justice and injustice do to the possessor of them. Example: The perfectly unjust may be 'deemed just when you are not' and able to profit; the perfectly just must be 'noble and simple' and not permitted to seem good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strip external reputation when testing moral worth
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be no seeming, for if he seem to be just he will be honoured and rewarded, and then we shall not know whether he is just for the sake of justice or for the sake of honours and rewards; therefore, let him be clothed in justice only, and have no other covering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating virtue in narrative, remove reputational incentives and honours so that a character's motives and internal goods are revealed. For an effective test, imagine the just man thought worst of men and the unjust man thought best; this isolates whether justice is chosen for its own sake rather than for appearance or rewards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use narrative reversal to probe character (appearances vs reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let him be the best of men, and let him be thought the worst; then he will have been put to the proof; and we shall see whether he will be affected by the fear of infamy and its consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce dramatic ironic reversals — e.g., a good person reputed evil, or an evil person reputed good — to reveal true motives and consequences. Such reversals function as an experiential test within the story and expose whether characters act for intrinsic goods or for appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with the larger (state) to illuminate the smaller (individual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice ... is sometimes spoken of as the virtue of an individual, and sometimes as the virtue of a State. And is not a State larger than an individual? Then in the larger the quantity of justice is likely to be larger and more easily discernible. I propose therefore that we enquire into the nature of justice and injustice, first as they appear in the State, and secondly in the individual, proceeding from the greater to the lesser and comparing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For complex moral topics, construct a large-scale setting (a city or society) to make structural principles visible, then translate those patterns to individual character. Worldbuilding can serve as an analytic device to reveal virtues/defects that are harder to see in single minds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worldbuilding must include plausible division of labor and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: A State arises out of the needs of mankind ... one man is a husbandman, another a builder, some one else a weaver ... carpenters, and smiths, and many other artisans ... merchants ... skilful sailors ... market-place, and a money-token for purposes of exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing a believable society, explicitly model specialization (one person one craft), markets, merchants, trade networks, money, and classes (artisans, retailers, hirelings). Show how economic needs generate roles and institutions; include details like marketplaces and the presence or absence of import/self-sufficiency to make the polity credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate 'healthy' and 'luxurious' states to show moral consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The true and healthy constitution of the State is the one which I have described. But if you wish also to see a State at fever-heat, ... add sofas, and tables, and other furniture; also dainties, and perfumes, and incense, and courtesans ... Then the city will have to fill and swell ... we shall want more servants ... the country which was enough to support the original inhabitants will be too small ... a slice of our neighbours' land will be wanted ... so we shall go to war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast a modest, necessity-based society with an expanded luxurious society to dramatize how surplus desires transform institutions and lead to conflict (e.g., expansion, war). Use escalation of wants and the resulting social specializations as a causal chain to explore ethical/political outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character/guardian selection: combine complementary traits
rubrics_metrics.description: He who is to be a really good and noble guardian of the State will require to unite in himself philosophy and spirit and swiftness and strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing archetypal guardians or protectors, give them a blend of intellectual virtues (love of wisdom) and bodily/spirited qualities (courage, speed, strength). Also attend to tensions (gentleness to friends vs fierceness to enemies) and show how such combinations are rare but possible (analogies given: well-bred dogs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure education: music (soul/literature) before gymnastics (body)
rubrics_metrics.description: The traditional sort has two divisions, gymnastic for the body, and music for the soul. Shall we begin education with music, and go on to gymnastic afterwards? ... And the young should be trained in both kinds, and we begin with the false? ... You know ... we begin by telling children stories which, though not wholly destitute of truth, are in the main fictitious; and these stories are told them when they are not of an age to learn gymnastics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In narratives about education, present formative moral instruction (myths, literature, songs) early in life because beginnings fix character. Use literature and music to shape desires and values before physical training; emphasize that early fictional narratives (even if partly fictive) have outsized formative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censor and authorize children's fiction deliberately
rubrics_metrics.description: Then the first thing will be to establish a censorship of the writers of fiction, and let the censors receive any tale of fiction which is good, and reject the bad; and we will desire mothers and nurses to tell their children the authorised ones only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If portraying a polity that cares about moral formation, include explicit controls on stories: a system of censors who vet tales for their moral suitability, and social practices that ensure only approved stories are told to children. When writing about education, make clear criteria for what counts as 'good' or 'bad' tales and show enforcement mechanisms (who decides, how authorized tales are distributed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat early narrative content as decisive in character formation
rubrics_metrics.description: You know also that the beginning is the most important part of any work, especially in the case of a young and tender thing; for that is the time at which the character is being formed and the desired impression is more readily taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize beginnings in story design and in diegetic educational practice: the tales, songs, and images young characters encounter should be chosen to instill desired virtues. In plotting, show how early exposures shape later moral choices; narratively, scenes of childhood instruction can plausibly explain adult dispositions.
